carrots-fresh-cooked-with-butter-or-marg.title: Carrots, fresh, cooked with butter or margarine

content.title: About
content.content: Carrots are root vegetables rich in beta‑carotene, which the body converts into vitamin A. Fresh carrots cooked with butter or margarine retain most nutrients and acquire a delicate buttery aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Carrots were domesticated in Central Asia over 5,000 years ago.
The orange color was popularized by Dutch breeders in the 17th century.
Raw carrot sticks are a common snack for children because of their soft texture.
Carrots grow in a wide range of climates, from temperate to subtropical regions.
There are more than 100 carrot varieties, including purple, yellow and red types.

items.title: Rich in beta‑carotene
items.content: Beta‑carotene is converted to vitamin A, supporting vision, immunity and skin health.

items.title: Cardiovascular support
items.content: Potassium and antioxidants help regulate blood pressure and reduce oxidative stress.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety and supports a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: One cup of sliced carrots contains about 40 kcal, making it a weight‑friendly food.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Flavonoids and carotenoids protect cells from free‑radical damage.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to carrots.

items.title: Excess vitamin A
items.content: Consuming extremely large amounts of carrots can lead to hypervitaminosis A, causing a yellowish skin tone.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: When buying non‑organic carrots, wash them thoroughly before cooking.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Carrots can be eaten raw, boiled, roasted, or sautéed in butter or margarine. Add them to salads, soups, stews, side dishes and casseroles. When sautéing, use a moderate amount of fat to preserve nutrients.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store carrots in the refrigerator’s vegetable drawer, placed in a perforated plastic bag or a container with a small amount of moisture. Cooked carrots sautéed in butter should be kept in an airtight container and consumed within 3–4 days.

cereal-or-granola-bar-quaker-chewy-25-le.title: Quaker Chewy 25% Less Sugar Granola Bar

content.title: About
content.content: Quaker Chewy 25% Less Sugar is a granola bar made by Quaker Oats. The bar contains whole oat flakes, nuts, dried fruit and flavorings, but the sugar amount is reduced by 25 % compared with the classic version. It is designed for a quick snack, provides sustained energy and is convenient on the go.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Quaker Chewy first appeared in the 1990s as a convenient snack for kids and adults.
The bar contains 30 % whole oat flakes, making it a good source of slowly digestible carbohydrates.
The reduced‑sugar version uses stevia as a sweetener to keep sweetness without extra calories.
Each bar is individually wrapped in recyclable film in most countries.
Quaker Oats is one of the oldest brands in the US, founded in 1901.

items.title: Reduced sugar content
items.content: A 25 % reduction in sugar helps control blood glucose levels and lowers the risk of excess calorie intake.

items.title: Source of whole grains
items.content: Oat flakes are rich in beta‑glucan, which supports heart health and improves digestion.

items.title: Contains nuts and dried fruit
items.content: Nuts provide healthy monounsaturated fats, while dried fruit adds vitamins and minerals such as potassium and iron.

items.title: Energy support
items.content: The combination of complex carbs and a modest amount of protein offers lasting satiety.

items.title: Convenient portion
items.content: Individual packaging allows easy portion control and makes the bar handy for bags or backpacks.

items.title: Nut and gluten allergy
items.content: The bar contains nuts and oats, so it may trigger reactions in people with those food allergies.

items.title: Sugar still present
items.content: Although reduced, sugar is still present, so individuals with diabetes should count it toward their daily intake.

items.title: Calorie density
items.content: One bar provides about 150 kcal, so it should be accounted for in a calorie‑controlled diet.

items.title: Artificial flavorings
items.content: The product may contain flavorings and preservatives that some consumers prefer to avoid.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The granola bar can be eaten straight out of the package, added to yogurt, sliced into cereal, or taken to the gym or on a trip. For a softer texture, you may warm it briefly in the microwave.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the bar in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, consume within 5‑7 days or transfer to an airtight container.

content.title: About
content.content: Edamame are young soybeans harvested before they fully mature and are usually served boiled or steamed in the pod. They have a mild, slightly sweet flavor and a pleasantly firm texture. Edamame are commonly eaten as a snack, added to salads, soups, and various Asian dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Edamame are a staple snack in Japan, China, and Korea, often served in bars and restaurants.
The soybeans used for edamame provide about 11 g of protein per 100 g of product.
In Japan they are traditionally sprinkled with sea salt, but they can also be flavored with spices, soy sauce, or garlic butter.
The Japanese name “edamame” (枝豆) means “beans on a branch.”
Edamame can be green or yellow depending on the soybean variety.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Edamame contain a complete set of essential amino acids, making them a valuable plant‑based protein source.

items.title: Good source of fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber supports digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Especially vitamin B6 and folate, which are important for metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: Edamame provide polyunsaturated fatty acids, including omega‑3s, that support cardiovascular health.

items.title: Mineral content
items.content: They supply iron, magnesium, potassium, and calcium, essential for bones and muscles.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: People allergic to soy may experience reactions ranging from mild to severe anaphylaxis.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce the absorption of certain minerals; moderate consumption is advised.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: High purine levels may be problematic for individuals with gout.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Edamame are typically served in the pod: bite the beans out and discard the pod. They can be enjoyed hot or cold, seasoned with salt, spices, or soy sauce. The beans also work well in salads, rice dishes, pasta, or as a puree.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked edamame in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Raw frozen beans keep for up to 6 months in the freezer.

content.title: About
content.content: Heart is a dietary supplement designed to support cardiovascular health. The formula combines vitamins, minerals, and plant extracts known for their beneficial effects on heart function and blood vessels.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The blend includes coenzyme Q10, which plays a key role in cellular energy production in the heart.
Olive leaf extract helps reduce oxidative stress.
Vitamin B6 and magnesium contribute to maintaining a normal heart rhythm.
The product is free from gluten, lactose, and artificial colourings.
Each package is formulated for a 30‑day daily regimen.

items.title: Supports energy metabolism
items.content: Coenzyme Q10 enhances ATP production in cardiomyocytes, boosting heart endurance.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Olive extract and vitamin E neutralise free radicals, reducing vascular damage.

items.title: Blood pressure regulation
items.content: Magnesium and potassium promote relaxation of vascular smooth muscle, helping maintain normal pressure.

items.title: Cholesterol reduction
items.content: Plant sterols in the formula help lower intestinal cholesterol absorption.

items.title: Nervous system support for heart rhythm
items.content: Vitamin B6 aids in the synthesis of neurotransmitters that influence cardiac rhythm.

items.title: Allergy to ingredients
items.content: The supplement contains plant extracts that may trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: Coenzyme Q10 can potentiate the effects of anticoagulants; consult a healthcare professional if you are on such medication.

items.title: Excessive dosage
items.content: High doses of magnesium may cause diarrhea and gastrointestinal discomfort.

items.title: Pregnancy and lactation
items.content: Safety during pregnancy and breastfeeding has not been established; it is advisable to avoid use.

content.title: How to Take
content.content: Take one capsule (or tablet) daily with a meal, accompanied by plenty of water. Do not exceed the recommended dose without medical advice.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a dry, cool place away from direct sunlight. Do not store above 30 °C. Shelf life is indicated on the packaging.

hot-dog-sandwich-meat-and-poultry-on-whe.title: Hot dog sandwich, meat and poultry, on wheat bun

content.title: About
content.content: A hot dog sandwich consists of a boiled or grilled meat‑and‑poultry sausage placed inside a soft wheat bun. It is often served with mustard, ketchup, mayonnaise, and various vegetable toppings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first commercial hot dog appeared in the United States in the late 19th century.
In the U.S., hot dogs are traditionally eaten with the hands, without a knife and fork.
Different countries use different types of sausage: Germany favors bratwurst, Japan uses teriyaki‑flavored sausages.
The wheat bun is usually lightly toasted to give a crisp exterior and a soft interior.
There is a “plain” version without toppings, focusing solely on the meat and bread flavors.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Meat‑and‑poultry sausage provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Red meat in the sausage is a good source of heme iron, which supports oxygen transport in the blood.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat products are rich in B12, B6, and niacin, which aid nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: The combination of protein, fat, and carbohydrates makes a hot dog a quick source of energy.

items.title: Calcium from the bun
items.content: A wheat bun, especially if fortified, adds a modest amount of calcium.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Sausages often contain a lot of salt, which can raise blood pressure when consumed frequently.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Meat products may be high in saturated fat, which can increase cholesterol levels.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The wheat bun contains gluten, which is unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Preservatives and additives
items.content: Some sausages contain nitrites and other preservatives that may be harmful in excess.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Hot dogs are usually eaten warm, split open lengthwise, and topped with sauces, mustard, ketchup, mayonnaise, pickles, onions, or sauerkraut. They are often served with french fries or a side salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the sausage in the refrigerator at 0 °C–4 °C, in its original packaging or an airtight container, and use within 3‑5 days after opening. Keep the bun in a dry place in a bag to prevent drying; for longer storage, refrigerate.

content.title: About
content.content: Mixed seeds are a blend of various edible seeds such as sunflower, pumpkin, flax, sesame and others. The mix is designed to provide a variety of flavors, textures and nutritional benefits. It can be eaten raw, added to salads, yogurts, cereals or used in baking.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sunflower seeds are rich in vitamin E and healthy fats.
Pumpkin seeds provide zinc, which supports the immune system.
Flaxseed is one of the best plant sources of omega‑3 fatty acids.
Sesame seeds are a staple in Asian cuisine and are used to make tahini.
Mixed seed blends are popular among athletes and vegetarians as a convenient source of plant protein.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Vitamin E and polyphenols in the seeds help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports heart health
items.content: Poly‑ and monounsaturated fats contribute to healthy cholesterol levels.

items.title: Provides plant protein
items.content: Seeds are a good source of protein needed for tissue repair and maintenance.

items.title: Packed with minerals
items.content: Calcium, magnesium, iron and zinc from seeds support bone health and metabolic functions.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: Fiber in the seeds promotes intestinal motility and a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to specific seeds, such as sesame.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Seeds are energy‑dense, so portion size should be monitored for weight management.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce the absorption of certain minerals; soaking or sprouting can mitigate this.

items.title: Contamination risk
items.content: Raw seeds may be contaminated with pathogens; when in doubt, heat‑treat them before consumption.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Mixed seeds can be enjoyed as a snack, sprinkled over yogurt, added to muesli, smoothies, salads, or incorporated into bread and bar doughs. Lightly toasting the seeds in a dry pan enhances flavor and digestibility.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the mix in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer shelf life keep it in the refrigerator to prevent fat oxidation. Discard seeds that develop a rancid smell.

moo-shu-pork-without-chinese-pancake.title: Moo Shu pork without Chinese pancake

content.title: About
content.content: Moo Shu pork is a Chinese‑style dish featuring stir‑fried pork tenderloin with vegetables, egg and soy sauce, served without the traditional thin pancakes. It offers a fragrant, slightly sweet flavor and tender meat texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish originated in Beijing in the early 20th century and quickly became popular in the United States.
Traditional Moo Shu is wrapped in wheat pancakes, but many people replace them with lettuce leaves for a lighter version.
Thinly sliced pork tenderloin is used, which keeps the meat exceptionally tender.
Shiitake mushrooms are often added in the classic recipe, giving the dish an earthy aroma.
Moo Shu pork is typically served “assembly‑style,” allowing diners to roll the ingredients themselves.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Pork tenderloin provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: The meat contains B1, B3 and B6 vitamins that support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Iron from pork helps form hemoglobin and prevents anemia.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: The dish fits low‑carb diets because most calories come from protein and fat.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Vegetables (carrot, cabbage, mushrooms) and soy sauce add antioxidants that support immunity.

items.title: Soy sauce allergy
items.content: Soy sauce can trigger allergic reactions in individuals with soy allergy.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce and added seasonings increase salt intake, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Risk of excess fat
items.content: Using too much oil for stir‑frying can make the dish calorie‑dense.

items.title: Undercooked pork hazard
items.content: Pork must be fully cooked to avoid salmonella or trichinella risk.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve Moo Shu pork on a plate and let each person wrap a portion in lettuce leaves or a gluten‑free rice paper. Add fresh cilantro, lime, and hot sauce to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the cooked dish to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2–3 days. Reheat quickly over high heat to keep the vegetables crisp.

content.title: About
content.content: Slim Fast Nutritional Protein Powder is a high‑protein blend designed to support weight management and maintain muscle mass. Provides 20 g of protein per serving, low in sugar, and fortified with vitamins and minerals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Available in several flavors: vanilla, chocolate, strawberry.
Each serving contains about 200 kcal, making it a convenient meal replacement.
The blend is based on whey protein, which is quickly absorbed.
Includes dietary fiber to promote satiety.
Slim Fast has been on the market for over 30 years and continuously updates its formula.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: 20 g of protein per serving helps maintain and rebuild muscle tissue.

items.title: Low sugar
items.content: Reduced sugar supports blood‑glucose control.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Fortified with vitamin D, calcium, and iron to support bone and immune health.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Aids digestion and prolongs feelings of fullness.

items.title: Convenient use
items.content: Easily dissolves in water, milk, or plant‑based drinks, ideal for on‑the‑go.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Whey protein may trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Artificial sweeteners
items.content: Some versions contain sucralose or aspartame, which some consumers prefer to avoid.

items.title: Not a complete meal substitute
items.content: Long‑term reliance solely on the powder may lead to nutrient gaps.

items.title: Possible gastrointestinal discomfort
items.content: Large protein doses can cause bloating or discomfort in people with sensitive GI tracts.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Mix one scoop (≈30 g) of powder with 250 ml of water, milk, or plant‑based beverage. For variety, add fruit, nuts, or oats.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place, tightly sealed. After opening, use within 3 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Pistachio nuts are the edible seeds of the pistachio tree (Pistacia vera), native to the Mediterranean region, Iran, the United States and other warm climates. They have a mildly sweet, buttery flavor and a crunchy texture. Pistachios are eaten raw, roasted, salted or used in cooking for pastes, desserts and baked goods.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pistachios belong to the cashew family and are close relatives of walnuts and sumac.
Mature nuts naturally split open, revealing the edible kernel without human intervention.
In ancient Persia pistachios were considered a delicacy and were often given as gifts.
There are two main commercial varieties: the dark‑green “Kerman” and the lighter “California” type.
Pistachios are a key ingredient in many Middle Eastern sweets such as baklava and katayef.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Pistachios contain vitamin E, polyphenols and carotenoids that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Provides healthy fats
items.content: The majority of fat in pistachios is monounsaturated, which supports heart health.

items.title: Source of protein and fiber
items.content: Pistachios supply plant protein and dietary fiber, promoting satiety and healthy digestion.

items.title: Supports eye health
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin found in pistachios are beneficial for vision and may reduce the risk of age‑related macular degeneration.

items.title: Contains essential minerals
items.content: Pistachios are a good source of potassium, magnesium and phosphorus, important for muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Tree nut allergy
items.content: Pistachios can trigger allergic reactions in individuals sensitive to nuts.

items.title: High in calories
items.content: Like most nuts, pistachios are calorie‑dense, so portion control is advised.

items.title: Salt and processing
items.content: Unsalted pistachios are preferred, as added salt can raise blood pressure.

items.title: Aflatoxin risk
items.content: Improper storage can lead to mold growth and aflatoxin production; keep nuts dry and cool.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pistachios can be enjoyed as a snack, tossed into salads, yogurts, oatmeal, baked goods, or processed into pistachio butter and pastes. They are frequently used in desserts, ice cream, and sauces. Unsalted pistachios are the healthiest choice.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store pistachios in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent oil oxidation. Discard nuts that smell rancid or stale.

content.title: About
content.content: Water is the fundamental component of an infant’s diet. For newborns and babies up to 6 months, only breast milk or specially formulated infant water without additives is recommended. From about 6 months, small amounts of boiled and cooled water can be introduced to support hydration.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pure water contains no calories, fat, protein, or carbohydrates.
For infants, low‑mineral (soft) water is preferred to avoid overloading the kidneys.
Boiling water for 1–2 minutes eliminates most bacteria and viruses.
Bottled baby water often contains added electrolytes, but these are needed only under specific medical advice.
Water that is too hot can cause burns, so it should be around 37 °C before feeding.

items.title: Maintains fluid balance
items.content: Water supports normal organ function, temperature regulation, and toxin elimination.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: Small amounts of water help soften stools and prevent constipation in babies.

items.title: Supports kidney development
items.content: Regular moderate water intake helps kidneys efficiently filter blood.

items.title: Mineral overload
items.content: Very hard water can lead to excess sodium and calcium intake, which is undesirable for an infant’s kidneys.

items.title: Contamination
items.content: Unverified water may contain bacteria, parasites, or chemical contaminants; always use tested or boiled water.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: Infants under 6 months should not be given water in a bottle to avoid aspiration risk.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: For children 6 months and older, offer small portions (30–60 ml) of boiled and cooled water in a clean bottle or cup. Do not add sugar, salt, or flavorings.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store boiled water in a sealed glass or food‑grade plastic container in the refrigerator for no more than 24 hours. Ensure the water is at room temperature before serving.
